title: Orthogonal matrices
summary: A real orthogonal matrix satisfies Q^T Q=I. Its columns are orthonormal, its inverse is its transpose, it preserves norms and dot products, and its determinant is 1 or -1.
intuition:
An orthogonal matrix is a square real matrix that preserves the geometry of $\mathbb{R}^n$. The defining equation is $Q^\top Q=I$. Reading it column by column, the columns are orthonormal: each has length $1$, and distinct columns have dot product $0$. The same equation says that $Q^\top$ is a left inverse, and for square matrices a left inverse is the two-sided inverse, so $Q^{-1}=Q^\top$ and also $QQ^\top=I$. The rows are orthonormal for the same reason.

Preservation is one line of algebra. For any vectors $x$ and $y$, $(Qx)\cdot(Qy)=x^\top Q^\top Q y=x^\top y$. Taking $x=y$ gives $\|Qx\|=\|x\|$. Rotations and reflections are the pictures: a rotation has determinant $1$, a reflection has determinant $-1$. There is no other possibility. From $Q^\top Q=I$ one gets $\det(Q)^2=\det(I)=1$, so $\det Q=\pm 1$.

An orthogonal matrix is not a projection. A projection satisfies $P^2=P$, while $Q^\top Q=I$ says that $Q$ is invertible. The only matrix that does both is $I$, because an orthogonal projection that is also orthogonal as a matrix has eigenvalues $0$ or $1$ and also eigenvalues of absolute value $1$, forcing every eigenvalue to be $1$. Orthogonal columns that are not unit length do not define an orthogonal matrix either: $Q^\top Q$ would be diagonal, but not the identity.

definitions.body: A square real matrix $Q$ is orthogonal when $Q^\top Q=I$. Then $Q^{-1}=Q^\top$, the columns are orthonormal, and the rows are orthonormal.
Columns $q_1,\ldots,q_n$ are orthonormal when $q_i^\top q_j$ is $1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Orthogonal columns of the wrong length are not enough.
Every real orthogonal matrix has $\det Q=\pm 1$. Determinant $1$ is a rotation in the plane; determinant $-1$ reverses orientation, as a reflection does.

formulas.name: Preserved dot product
formulas.note: Set $y=x$ to get $\|Qx\|=\|x\|$. Lengths and angles both survive.

properties: $Q^\top Q=I$, so the columns are orthonormal and $Q^{-1}=Q^\top$. The rows are orthonormal because $QQ^\top=I$ as well.
$\|Qx\|=\|x\|$ and $(Qx)\cdot(Qy)=x\cdot y$ for every pair of real vectors.
$\det Q=\pm 1$. The square of the determinant is $\det(Q^\top Q)=\det I=1$.
A product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal, and the inverse of an orthogonal matrix is orthogonal.
An orthogonal matrix is not a projection matrix, except for $I$. A projection satisfies $P^2=P$; an orthogonal matrix satisfies $Q^\top Q=I$.

examples.title: A quarter turn
examples.prompt: Let $Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Check $Q^\top Q=I$, compute $\det Q$ and $Q^{-1}$, and apply $Q$ to $(3,4)^\top$.
steps: The determinant is $(0)(0)-(-1)(1)=1$, which is one of the two legal values $\pm 1$.

$Q\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\3\end{pmatrix}$. Both vectors have squared length $9+16=25$, so the Euclidean norm is preserved. Also $Q^2=-I\neq Q$, so this orthogonal matrix is not a projection.
examples.answer: $Q$ is orthogonal with $\det Q=1$ and $Q^{-1}=Q^\top$. It sends $(3,4)$ to $(-4,3)$, both of norm $5$.

examples.title: A reflection, and a matrix that only looks orthogonal
examples.prompt: Let $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Which one is orthogonal? Compute $R^2$ and $B^\top B$.
steps: $R^\top=R$ and $R^\top R=I$, so $R$ is orthogonal. Its determinant is $-1$.
$R^2=I$, which is not $R$. An orthogonal projection would have satisfied $P^2=P$. This reflection is orthogonal and it is not a projection.

The columns of $B$ are orthogonal, but $B^\top B=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\neq I$ and $\det B=2$, which is not $\pm 1$. Orthogonal columns of the wrong length do not make an orthogonal matrix.
examples.answer: $R$ is orthogonal, $\det R=-1$, and $R^2=I\neq R$. The diagonal matrix $B$ is not orthogonal.

traps: Calling a matrix orthogonal because its columns are perpendicular. They also have to be unit vectors. $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has perpendicular columns and $Q^\top Q\neq I$.
Confusing an orthogonal matrix with an orthogonal projection. The projection equation is $P^2=P=P^\top$. The orthogonal-matrix equation is $Q^\top Q=I$. Only $I$ satisfies both.
Thinking the determinant of an orthogonal matrix can be any number of absolute value $1$ in a loose sense, or that it must be $+1$. Both signs occur: a rotation has $+1$ and a reflection has $-1$.
Using $Q^{-1}=Q$ instead of $Q^{-1}=Q^\top$. Those agree only when $Q$ is symmetric, as a reflection through a coordinate axis is, and a quarter turn is not.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

def T(A):
    return [list(row) for row in zip(*A)]

Q = [[0, -1], [1, 0]]
I = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]
assert mul(T(Q), Q) == I
det = Q[0][0] * Q[1][1] - Q[0][1] * Q[1][0]
assert det == 1
Qx = [Q[0][0] * 3 + Q[0][1] * 4, Q[1][0] * 3 + Q[1][1] * 4]
assert Qx == [-4, 3]
assert Qx[0] ** 2 + Qx[1] ** 2 == 25
R = [[1, 0], [0, -1]]
assert mul(R, R) == I
assert R[0][0] * R[1][1] - R[0][1] * R[1][0] == -1
print(25)

questions.stem: A real square matrix $Q$ is orthogonal when
options: the columns are perpendicular, with no condition on their lengths
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. The equation $Q^\top Q=I$ forces the columns to be orthonormal and forces $Q^{-1}=Q^\top$. Option B is idempotence, the projection and idempotent-matrix condition. Symmetry is not required: a quarter turn is orthogonal and not symmetric. Perpendicular columns of the wrong length fail $Q^\top Q=I$.

questions.stem: The determinant of a real orthogonal matrix is
questions.solution: The answer is **C**. From $Q^\top Q=I$, take determinants: $\det(Q)^2=1$, so $\det Q=\pm 1$. Both signs occur. The quarter turn $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $1$, and the reflection $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-1$. An orthogonal matrix is invertible, so the determinant is not $0$.

questions.stem: Let $Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. Direct multiplication gives $Q^\top Q=I$, so the inverse equals the transpose, and $\det Q=(0)(0)-(-1)(1)=1$. But $Q^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}=-I$, which is not $Q$. This orthogonal matrix is not a projection.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: An orthogonal matrix preserves the Euclidean norm.
An orthogonal matrix preserves the dot product.
Every orthogonal projection matrix is an orthogonal matrix.
The columns of an orthogonal matrix are orthonormal.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and D**. The identity $(Qx)^\top(Qy)=x^\top Q^\top Q y=x^\top y$ preserves dot products, and the case $y=x$ preserves norms. The columns are orthonormal by $Q^\top Q=I$. C is false: a projection of rank less than the ambient dimension has determinant $0$, while an orthogonal matrix has determinant $\pm 1$. Only $I$ is both.

The answer is **25**. First $Qx=(-4,3)^\top$, and $(-4)^2+3^2=16+9=25$. The same number is $\|x\|^2=9+16$, which is the general fact that an orthogonal matrix preserves Euclidean length. The square of the length is the integer the question asks for.
